### Step 1: Research Question and Context

In this project, I investigate whether IMDb ratings for TV shows differ between male-identifying and female-identifying reviewers in the larger population of TV viewers, not just in this dataset. The “IMDb_Economist_tv_ratings.csv” dataset comes from The Economist (via TidyTuesday Week 2, 2019) and includes TV show titles, average IMDb ratings, and gender-split rating data.

We want to understand whether the small differences observed in this dataset could reasonably occur from random chance alone. To answer this, we simulate a world where gender has no role in how people rate TV shows. Under that null hypothesis, any difference we see in average ratings would simply be due to natural variability from sample to sample.

Our goal:\
“Is the difference we observe in our dataset larger than we would normally expect if the underlying rating tendency were the same for everyone?”

### Step 2: Setup and Data Cleaning

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

tv <- read_csv("IMDb_Economist_tv_ratings.csv")

#constructing the gender comparison dataset

set.seed(47)

ratings_sim <- tv |> 
  filter(!is.na(av_rating)) |> 
  mutate(gender = sample(c("Male", "Female"), 
                         size = n(), replace = TRUE))

#observed statistic: difference in mean ratings
ratings_sim |> 
  group_by(gender) |> 
  summarize(mean_rating = mean(av_rating)) |> 
  summarize(obs_diff = diff(mean_rating)) |> 
  pull()

#defining a permutation function

perm_data <- function(rep, data){
  data |> 
    mutate(gender_perm = sample(gender, replace = FALSE)) |> 
    group_by(gender_perm) |> 
    summarize(mean_rating = mean(av_rating)) |> 
    summarize(perm_diff = diff(mean_rating)) |> 
    pull()
}

#simulate the null sampling distribution

set.seed(47)
num_exper <- 5000

perm_results <- map_dbl(1:num_exper, perm_data, data = ratings_sim)

#p value

obs_diff <- ratings_sim |> 
  group_by(gender) |> 
  summarize(mean_rating = mean(av_rating)) |> 
  summarize(diff = diff(mean_rating)) |> 
  pull()

p_value <- mean(perm_results >= obs_diff)
p_value

#visualizing the null distribution

perm_results |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = perm_results)) + 
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "blue", color = "black") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = obs_diff), color = "orange", linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +
  labs(
    x = "Simulated difference in mean rating (Female - Male)",
    title = "Sampling distribution under the null hypothesis",
    subtitle = "No relationship between reviewer gender and rating"
  )

```

### Step 3: Interpretation:

The histogram shows what differences in average ratings we would expect just by chance if gender were unrelated to TV show ratings in the broader viewer population. The orange dashed line marks the difference we observed in the dataset. Because the observed value lies near the center of the simulated null distribution, differences of this size would be very common even if gender truly had no effect. Therefore, our observed difference is not unusual under the null hypothesis.

### Step 4: Conclusions

This permutation test evaluates whether the difference in TV show ratings between male and female reviewers seen in this dataset is larger than what would be expected from normal random variation. Because the observed difference aligns closely with the null distribution, we do not have evidence that rating tendencies differ by gender in the broader population of IMDb users. This does not prove that gender will never matter, rather, based on the dataset available, any differences we observe could easily be explained by chance alone.
